paragraphs: Scope and boundaries: this page covers only O*NET-SOC 51-4072.00, Molding, Coremaking, and Casting Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic, excluding adjacent occupations such as nonmetallic forming, machining, and tool and die making. Employer and local rules determine safety and operating authorization for furnaces, die-casting equipment, hot work, and lifting.

How to assess: use an entirely fictional work order and process sheet to sequence work order interpretation and mold selection and installation, mold and equipment preparation, parameter settings and trial molding, operation monitoring and measurement, demolding and finishing, and records and handover. Describe three checkpoints and anomaly responses. Perform paper exercises only, without real furnaces, die-casting machines, or molds.

Who it suits: people willing to repeatedly verify work orders and parameters, notice surface and dimensional deviations, maintain attention at machine pace and record as required, and stop equipment to seek verification when jams, overtemperature, or dimensional anomalies arise. Note: if heat, noise, or repetitive movements are difficult to tolerate, or you are unwilling to stop equipment and seek verification, compare adjacent directions first.

Note: the following are editorially designed paper exercises without real melts, molds, or employer production data. They do not authorize equipment operation, hot work, lifting, or quality release. Judgments involving safety, health, and qualifications require employer procedures and local rules.

The official scope of O*NET-SOC 51-4072.00, Molding, Coremaking, and Casting Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic, is setting up, operating, or tending metal or plastic molding, casting, or coremaking machines to form metal or thermoplastic materials into parts or products. Excludes machinists who cut materials, tool and die makers who make molds, and workers molding and carving nonmetallic materials.

entries: Work order interpretation and mold selection and installation: read specifications, drawings, and work orders to determine mold setup, temperatures, and times and plan production sequences. Mount and secure molds on machines or presses, clean and lubricate mold interiors, fill defects with refractory material, and connect mold cooling water lines.

Parameter settings and trial molding: adjust valves and knobs to control pressure, temperature, speed, and feed and set cycle times. Select and install blades and tool attachments, adjust workholding devices, apply release agents, and conduct trial molding for confirmation.

Operation monitoring and measurement review: observe continuous automated equipment operation, record temperatures, pressures, and injection cycles using instruments and gauges, and adjust for jams or faults. Remove and cool products, trim excess material, inspect surface and dimensional defects visually and with instruments, count quantities, record batches, and hand over.

paragraphs: Work context (O*NET Work Context survey): 59% of respondents encounter minor burns, cuts, stings, or bites daily; 53% report machine speed completely determines work pace, with another 23% rating it very important. 39% have continual contact with others and 33% contact most of the time. 77% never sit at work, 92% never need to face external customers or the public, and 92% never work outdoors under cover.

Capability priorities: understand work orders and drawings, install molds and adjust parameters according to process sheets, monitor operation and record temperatures and pressures, review dimensions and appearance visually and with instruments, and stop to seek verification for jams, overtemperature, or abnormal parameters. Requires metal or plastic material, mold, and equipment knowledge and procedural recordkeeping habits.

Preparation and training: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone 1—2, generally requiring a high school diploma or equivalent, as reported by 57% of education survey respondents. Related experience ranges from almost none to several months—one year; on-the-job training ranges from several days to one year (SVP below 6.0). No training programs were found nationwide.

Occupational judgments: key decisions concern mold-material compatibility, correct temperature and pressure parameters, first-article conformity, and product dimensional and appearance conformity. Stop equipment and escalate first when uncertain or beyond authorization.
Main outputs: conforming castings or plastic products, traceable mold and process parameter records, temperature and pressure curves, and dimensional and appearance review results.

Complete work cycle: work order interpretation and mold selection and installation, mold and equipment preparation, parameter settings and trial molding, operation monitoring and measurement, demolding and finishing, dimensional and appearance review, maintenance, and records and handover. Each step requires verifiable evidence.

Conclusion: this occupation's core outputs are parts or products made using metal or plastic molding, casting, and coremaking equipment. Nonmetallic forming workers mold and carve nonmetallic materials, foundry mold and coremakers specialize in sand molds and cores, machinists and tool and die makers focus on cutting and moldmaking, and welding and cutting workers focus on joining processes. Adjacent relationships support comparisons only, not automatic transfers or mutual recognition of qualifications.
Comparisons use the official O*NET 51-4072.00 description and tasks and adjacent O*NET occupational profiles. This is an editorial synthesis, not job recommendations.
Comparison dimensions: this page compares core work and outputs, key differences from this occupation, and which choices may fit better, to help assess directional preferences.

Difference from Molders, Shapers, and Casters, Except Metal and Plastic: this occupation operates metal or plastic molding, casting, and coremaking machines and handles melts and mold closing. The adjacent occupation primarily molds, shapes, and carves nonmetallic materials such as clay, glass, plaster, concrete, and stone.

If you prefer specializing in sand molds and cores with less high-pressure mold closing, compare foundry mold and coremakers; if you prefer precision cutting to drawings, compare machinists; if you prefer making and repairing molds themselves, compare tool and die makers.
People entering the field and trial molding
First verify process sheets, mold numbers, and safety procedures. Complete mold installation and trial molding under guidance without skipping equipment operation and hot-work authorization.
Workers primarily in die casting, injection molding, and batch production

Include parameter versions, mold numbers, temperature and pressure curves, and first-article decisions in review points. Handle anomalies according to shutdown and escalation rules and retain audit trails.
Personnel responsible for processes and mentoring
Base mentoring on verifiable outputs and records, reserving parameter change and appearance standard decisions for authorized personnel under employer procedures.
Career changers
Develop material, mold, and measurement fundamentals first, then accumulate process records through public or simulated projects. Do not treat generated content as capability evidence.

Insufficient evidence: a national wage distribution in mainland China for metal/plastic molding, coremaking, and casting equipment operation has not been obtained. NBS2025 manufacturing and production/manufacturing group averages are related references, not this occupation's wages.

Scope comparison: the National Bureau of Statistics publishes average wages of urban unit employees by industry category without separately identifying 'casting workers' or corresponding metal/plastic molding equipment occupations.

Verifiable reference: 2025 manufacturing average annual wages were 113,594 yuan/year in urban non-private units (nominal growth 5.2%) and 76,055 yuan/year in urban private units (nominal growth 6.4%). Coverage includes urban legal entities with 5 or more employees, excluding individual businesses and freelancers.

Insufficient evidence: a national wage distribution in mainland China for metal/plastic molding, coremaking, and casting equipment operation has not been obtained. NBS2025 manufacturing and production/manufacturing group averages are related references, not this occupation's wages.

Boundaries: this checklist is an editorial synthesis and cannot replace employer safety procedures, furnace and press operating procedures, or local regulations. Specific protection, exposure limits, and authorization depend on relevant authority and employer documents.

The main issues to assess in advance are burns from molten metal and hot castings, foundry dust and silica exposure, moving equipment parts and pinch injuries, and batch scrap from incorrect parameters or mold setups. Exposure points differ across mold installation and parameter adjustment, operation and monitoring, and review and delivery.

Evidence scope: dust and respiratory health references U.S. CDC/NIOSH silica and occupational health materials; machine and equipment guarding references relevant U.S. OSHA 29 CFR 1910 standards. Work context percentages reflect U.S. O*NET respondents and are not extrapolated to other regions.
Affected roles and tasks: personnel performing melting, pouring, coremaking, shakeout, sand removal, and surface finishing.

Hot materials involve burn exposure. Dust containing respirable crystalline silica is associated with silicosis, lung cancer, COPD, and kidney disease; this does not refer to all dust or plastic molding.

Boundaries: entry paths and capability stages on this page are editorial organization explaining preparation order, not standardized industry levels or guaranteed promotion timelines. Verify skills and safety requirements for furnaces, die-casting equipment, hot work, and lifting against employer procedures and local rules.
Entry stage: can understand work orders and drawings under guidance, clean and lubricate molds, apply release agents, perform simple mold installations, and truthfully record and report difficulties.

Process and mentoring stage: can lead process parameters, molds, and appearance standards and mentor others within authorization, without replacing employer safety and quality sign-off responsibilities.

risks.mitigation: Use fixtures and thermal protection, follow preheating and cooling procedures, provide warnings and interlocks, and receive hot-work training
risks.scenario: Contact with molten metal, hot casting molds, and dies during pouring, skimming, and part removal
risks.title: Burns from molten metal and hot castings

risks.affected_roles: Personnel performing coremaking, shakeout, sand removal, and surface finishing
risks.consequence: Associated with risks including silicosis, lung cancer, COPD, and chronic kidney impairment
risks.mitigation: Provide ventilation, enclosure, monitoring, and protection according to dust assessments. Wet controls must not conflict with molten metal contact risks; specific controls follow safety and process procedures.
risks.scenario: Handling sand molds or cores containing crystalline silica, sand removal, and grinding may generate respirable dust. Plastic molding does not automatically involve the same exposure.
risks.title: Foundry dust and silica exposure

risks.affected_roles: Personnel installing molds, adjusting parameters, and cleaning molds
risks.consequence: May cause pinch injuries, cuts, and crushing injuries
risks.mitigation: Follow lockout/tagout and guarding procedures; do not remove guards or bypass interlocks
risks.scenario: Approaching presses, molds, and transmission parts during mold installation, machine adjustment, mold cleaning, and part removal
risks.title: Moving equipment parts and pinch injuries

risks.affected_roles: Personnel installing molds, adjusting parameters, and conducting trial molding
risks.consequence: May require entire batches to be scrapped or reworked and affect delivery and acceptance
risks.mitigation: Confirm first articles, check molds, document parameters and curves, and reinspect using instruments before batch production
risks.scenario: Misread mold numbers or process parameters and unsuitable temperature and pressure settings cause shrinkage cavities, missing material, or deformation
risks.title: Incorrect parameter and mold setups causing batch scrap

risks.affected_roles: Personnel installing molds, removing parts, and handling materials
risks.consequence: Official surveys support standing and machine-paced work context. Insufficient evidence: body-part strain or hearing outcome research for this occupation has not been obtained; context does not establish disease causation.
risks.mitigation: Rotate tasks, use handling aids and adjustable work surfaces, wear hearing protection, and schedule appropriate breaks
risks.scenario: Prolonged standing, lifting molds, and repetitive movements in hot and noisy environments
risks.title: Heat, noise, and repetitive movement strain

risks.affected_roles: Personnel responsible for process records and handovers
risks.consequence: Difficult to establish conformity or trace batches, increasing rework and claim risks
risks.mitigation: Record mold, parameter, temperature, and measurement data according to standards and retain versions and deviations
risks.scenario: Failing to record mold numbers, process parameters, temperatures, and measured dimensions or document rework decisions
risks.title: Incomplete parameter and batch records

description.text: Casting workers (O*NET 51-4072.00) set up and tend metal and plastic molding, casting, and coremaking equipment, die-casting, pouring, coremaking, and demolding parts. This page explains official tasks and work context, the U.S. BLS 2025 median wage of 44,350 USD and 4% decline for 2024—2034, mainland Chinese manufacturing and broad production/manufacturing job category proxy wages, AI task boundaries, fit signals, and entry paths.

subject.name: Casting workers
subject.summary: Molding, Coremaking, and Casting Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic (O*NET 51-4072.00) set up, operate, or tend equipment that forms metal or thermoplastic materials into parts or products. Work centers on work order interpretation and mold selection and installation, pressure, temperature, and cycle control, operation observation and measurement, demolding and finishing, and records and handover.
